entity.name: Molière
entity.description: The playwright who died onstage playing a hypochondriac. France's greatest comic writer spent 13 years as a traveling actor before winning Louis XIV's patronage. His satires of religious hypocrisy got banned by the Church; the French language itself is still called "the language of Molière."

story.name: Molière
story.description: A wine merchant's son founds a theater troupe that goes bankrupt, spends 13 years touring provincial France, wins Louis XIV's favor, gets Tartuffe banned by the Church, and collapses onstage during his final performance.

moments.name: Molière Abandons a Privileged Life to Found a Theater Troupe
moments.subtitle: A 21-year-old trades a royal upholstery post for a stage career that lands him in prison
moments.description: In June 1643, Jean-Baptiste Poquelin — later known as Molière — gave up his inherited position as valet to the King's chamber and joined actress Madeleine Béjart to found the Illustre Théâtre in Paris with 630 livres. The venture was a financial disaster. By 1645 the troupe owed 2,000 livres in rent and Molière spent 24 hours in debtor's prison. It was after this humiliation that he adopted his stage name, possibly to spare his father the shame of having an actor in the family. The failure launched 13 years of provincial touring that would forge France's greatest comic voice.

moments.name: Molière Performs for Louis XIV and Wins Royal Patronage
moments.subtitle: A provincial actor gambles everything on one night at the Louvre — and wins
moments.description: In October 1658, Molière performed before King Louis XIV at the Louvre, staging Corneille's tragedy Nicomède followed by his own farce Le Docteur Amoureux. The king was sufficiently impressed to grant Molière's company the title Troupe de Monsieur and permission to share the Petit-Bourbon theater with an Italian commedia dell'arte troupe. This royal favor transformed a touring provincial company into the most celebrated theater troupe in France. Molière would go on to become the official author of court entertainments, and his plays remain the most performed works at the Comédie-Française to this day.

moments.name: The Catholic Church Gets Molière's Tartuffe Banned in Paris
moments.subtitle: A comedy about religious hypocrisy proves so accurate that the hypocrites ban it
moments.description: In 1664, Molière premiered Tartuffe, a savage comedy about a pious fraud who manipulates a gullible household. The Catholic Church in France denounced the play as an attack on religion itself, and the Parlement of Paris imposed a formal ban. Molière spent five years fighting to get the play restaged, writing petitions to Louis XIV and revising the script. The ban was finally lifted in 1669, and Tartuffe became one of the most performed plays in French history. The controversy cemented Molière's reputation as a fearless satirist willing to challenge the most powerful institutions in France.

moments.name: Molière Premieres Les Précieuses Ridicules and Mocks Parisian Society
moments.subtitle: The first of many plays that made the elite furious and the public delighted
moments.description: On 18 November 1659, Molière premiered Les Précieuses Ridicules (The Affected Young Ladies) at the Petit-Bourbon theater in Paris. The one-act comedy ruthlessly satirized the pretentious mannerisms of Parisian high society and mocked the Académie Française's rigid rules for theater. It was Molière's first major satirical work and established the template for his career: comedies that held a mirror to social absurdity. The play drew both attention and fierce criticism from the upper classes it lampooned, setting the pattern of controversy that would follow Molière for the rest of his life.

moments.name: Molière Collapses Onstage Playing a Hypochondriac and Dies Hours Later
moments.subtitle: The greatest irony in theater history: a dying man performing a comedy about fake illness
moments.description: On 17 February 1673, Molière took the stage at the Palais-Royal to play Argan, the title character in his final comedy The Imaginary Invalid — a hypochondriac who believes he is gravely ill. Molière, who actually suffered from pulmonary tuberculosis, was seized by a violent coughing fit and hemorrhage during the fourth performance. He finished the show but collapsed again afterward and died at his home a few hours later, at age 51. Because actors were denied Christian burial, Molière's wife had to petition Louis XIV just to have him interred in consecrated ground — at night, with no ceremony.
